newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD offers olive branch on German reforms.
newsitem.headline: SPD offers olive branch on German reforms.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Tuesday offered to help haul Chancellor Helmut Kohl out of a pensions policy mire -- but only after his own three-party coalition has agreed a common line on reforms.
SPD leaders rushed, however, to quell speculation they were ready to form a grand coalition with Kohl, who last week called for cross-party talks to reshape the tax and pensions systems.
"We are not talking about a grand coalition, but about finding a consensus between the parties on the pensions issue," SPD deputy chairman Wolfgang Thierse told Middle German Radio.

SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told reporters that Kohl would first have to restore order in coalition ranks before talks could go ahead. He added the SPD would finalise its own pensions position by early March.
"Everything will be clear after that," Scharping said.

The SPD pensions offer follows up tax counter-proposals it made on Monday, accepting coalition plans for a new 15 percent income tax entry rate, but rejecting cutting the top rate to 39 percent and ruling out raising value-added tax.

The moves appear timed to catch Kohl's 14-year-old alliance when it is most vulnerable. Rumbling coalition unrest burst into the open last week after Labour Minister Norbert Bluem announced proposals to rejig the state pensions scheme.

Bluem -- a minister since Kohl came to power in 1982 -- angered his coalition colleagues by not consulting them on his plans and demanding a hike in VAT to set up a "family fund" to pay for non-related welfare benefits.

The proposals run headlong into parallel coalition tax reforms drawn up under Finance Minister Theo Waigel -- who opposes raising VAT to fund benefits and wants to tax pensions in a package which would cut 30 billion marks in taxes.
Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) managed to regroup on Monday, when 20 out of 28 party pensions experts backed the Bluem plan, with minor changes, at a brainstorming session.
The group hardly touched Bluem's proposals to cut pensions to 64 percent of average net wages by 2030 from 70 percent now and raise contributions to 22.9 percent from 20.3 percent.

The CDU executive will discuss the pensions plan on Wednesday, and although Bluem has won the backing of senior party allies, there is still widespread discontent -- both in the party and the coalition -- over his plans.
"The hymns of praise from Bluem's friends...cannot hide the unhappiness of the coalition as a whole over the proposals," Die Welt newspaper commented on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, mere talk of a grand coalition being formed ahead of parliamentary elections next year has dampened, but not silenced, criticism of Bluem from Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP).
"The FDP has nothing against Norbert Bluem," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle said. "But we do oppose a pensions policy under which the next generation picks up the tab."

FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt also rallied behind Kohl: "This Chancellor is a guarantor for the coalition. We agree on tax, pensions and European policy and want to deal with these tasks together," he said.
Back at the headquarters of Kohl's CDU, party strategists were more cheerful than they have been in over a week over the SPD's readiness for dialogue.
"The SPD has realised what it has to do," one said.

Doubts remain, however, over whether the SPD will adopt a constructive negotiating position. That would mean giving up its biggest political weapon -- the power to veto tax measures through its majority in the upper house of parliament.
